newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria leader urges Socialists to refuse mandate.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria leader urges Socialists to refuse mandate.

text.p: Bulgarian President Petar Stoyanov said on Monday he would give the ruling Socialists a mandate to form a new government but urged them to return it and agree to opposition demands for a quick general election.

As daily protest rallies against the Socialists entered their fourth week, he urged the opposition to abandon its boycott of parliament and called on both parties to cooperate in a 10-day legislative programme to pass measures to tackle the economic crisis.

"The United Democratic Forces should show understanding and temporarily return to the parliament. The deputies from the Left should also give ground and refuse the mandate which they will receive from me in the name of consensus," Stoyanov said in a broadcast statement.
"The active work of the deputies will allow elections to be held as early as possible."

Under the constitution Stoyanov is obliged to ask the ex-communist Socialists, as the biggest party in parliament, to form a new cabinet. If all parties fail to form a government, elections should be held within two months.

Since taking office last Wednesday the president has tried to negotiate a consensus. But the two sides remain as far apart as ever and he has promised to give the Socialists a mandate before he leaves on a trip to Brussels on Tuesday.

Some 2,000 students with white-painted faces held a "March of the Dead" in Sofia. Blowing whistles and shaking cans full of worthless lev coins, they marched from the university to join the main opposition rally.
At the Alexander Nevsky cathedral, the estimated 18,000 protesters included a group of miners with helmets and lamps. "I'm here because I'm hungry and I'm angry" said one banner.
Opposition leader Ivan Kostov told the crowd Stoyanov had appealed to all parliamentary groups to refuse a mandate and set a deadline of 12.30 p.m. on Tuesday for their response.
"Once again I have to appeal to all of you to have the courage and the persistence to win our battle," he said.
Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov offered little hope of compromise, repeating that a cabinet of technocrats led by Socialist Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev offered the best solution to the crisis.
"I continue to insist that the nomination of Nikolai Dobrev is the best possibility," he told reporters.
Dobrev is unacceptable to the opposition who hold him responsible for clashes between police and demonstrators outside parliament on January 10.

If parliament votes on a new Socialist cabinet, the opposition will be pinning its hopes on defections from the majority party. The vote is almost certain to attract demonstrations, which risk turning violent again.

The protests are more economic than political, and an opinion poll in the 24 Hours daily on Monday said 70 percent of those questioned did not trust the Socialists but 35 percent did not think the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces could cope with the crisis either.

The national currency is in freefall and January inflation is expected to hit 50 percent a month. The lev closed at 935-945 to the dollar on the interbank market on Monday, compared to about 750 a week earlier.

Bulgaria urgently needs a credible government to negotiate a new accord with the International Monetary Fund, which has suspended disbursements because the Socialist government of Zhan Videnov, which resigned on December 21, failed to implement the last reform programme.
